tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Success depends of careful practice before the recital.
She is responsible of watering the neighbour's plants.
They are interested on learning Portuguese this summer.
Despite of the rain, the picnic went ahead.
He was accused of cheating in the board-game tournament.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use depends on, not depends of, for this fixed dependency pattern.

Tip: After depend, lock in on — of is a common L1 transfer trap.

FALSE — Use responsible for, not responsible of.

Tip: Pair responsible with for + noun/gerund; of is wrong here.

FALSE — The fixed pattern is interested in, not interested on.

Tip: Interest takes in; on belongs with focus/concentrate.

FALSE — Despite never takes of; write Despite the rain or In spite of the rain.

Tip: Despite of is always wrong — drop of or switch to in spite of.

TRUE — Accused of + gerund/noun is the standard collocation.

Tip: Accuse/charge of wrongdoing; do not swap in for after accused.
tasks.solution_overview: Scan each sentence for a fixed verb/adjective + preposition lock. Ask whether the preposition matches the standard pattern, and watch for the classic despite of false friend.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He insisted on seeing the raw score sheets.
Her recipe differs of last year's version.
We apologised about spilling juice on the carpet.
The documentary focuses to ocean plastics.
She participated in the weekend pottery workshop.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Insist on + gerund is the fixed pattern here.

Tip: After insist, use on + -ing, not a bare infinitive.

FALSE — Use differs from, not differs of.

Tip: Differ/different → from; do not write differ of.

FALSE — Prefer apologised for spilling… in careful exam English.

Tip: Apologise for a fault or inconvenience; about is weaker and often marked wrong.

FALSE — Use focuses on, not focuses to.

Tip: Focus/concentrate take on, never to.

TRUE — Participated in correctly names involvement in an event.

Tip: Participate/join/engage → in an event or activity.
tasks.solution_overview: These items test high-frequency everyday collocations. Match each verb to its locked preposition, and rewrite any false friend before deciding TRUE or FALSE.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: They objected against the new quiet-hours rule.
The volunteer is capable of handling the front desk.
She is good in swimming long distances.
We look forward to meeting your cousins.
He succeeded to repair the bicycle chain.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Object takes to, not against: objected to the rule.

Tip: Object to X; protest against is a different verb.

TRUE — Capable of + gerund is the fixed ability pattern.

Tip: Capable of doing; able to do — different frames.

FALSE — Use good at swimming, not good in for skills.

Tip: Good/bad/skilled at activities; in is for subjects like good in maths only in some varieties — exam English prefers at for skills.

TRUE — Look forward to + gerund (meeting) is correct; to is a preposition here.

Tip: After look forward to, use a noun or -ing, never a bare infinitive.

FALSE — Succeed in repairing, not succeed to repair.

Tip: Succeed in + -ing; manage to + infinitive is the other pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Check object to, capable of, good at, look forward to + -ing, and succeed in. Wrong prepositions or infinitives after these heads are almost always FALSE.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The salad consists from tomatoes, cucumber, and feta.
This jacket belongs to my older brother.
You can rely of her to bring the tent.
They complained for the noisy neighbours upstairs.
A locked gate prevented them from entering the park.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Consist of lists the parts; consist from is wrong.

Tip: Consist of / be made of — not from after consist.

TRUE — Belong to correctly marks ownership.

Tip: Belong to someone; never belong of.

FALSE — Use rely on, not rely of.

Tip: Rely/depend/count → on.

FALSE — Complain about a problem; complain for is non-standard here.

Tip: Complain about noise/service; complain to a person.

TRUE — Prevent someone from + gerund is the fixed restraint pattern.

Tip: Prevent/stop/keep from doing; not to do after prevent.
tasks.solution_overview: Everyday ownership and hindrance verbs lock tightly: consist of, belong to, rely on, complain about, prevent from. Mark any swapped preposition false.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Lisbon is famous for its tiled façades.
This trail is similar with the one near the lake.
My playlist is different than yours in every genre.
She has been married with her partner for twelve years.
The children are afraid of thunderstorms at night.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Famous for + noun phrase is the standard reputation pattern.

Tip: Famous/known for a feature; famous as a role.

FALSE — Similar to, not similar with.

Tip: Similar/identical/comparable → to.

FALSE — In careful exam English prefer different from (or different to in BrE); different than is often marked down.

Tip: Different from is the safest exam choice.

FALSE — Married to a person, not married with.

Tip: Married to someone; with belongs in other frames (live with).

TRUE — Afraid of + noun is correct.

Tip: Afraid of something; frightened of works the same way.
tasks.solution_overview: Adjective + preposition pairs are rigid: famous for, similar to, different from, married to, afraid of. Swap the preposition and the sentence fails.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We arrived to the station just before midnight.
Please listen to the podcast episode I sent.
They waited the bus for twenty minutes in the rain.
Look at the mural behind the café.
We talked the film for almost an hour.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Arrive at a station/building; arrive in a city/country — not arrive to.

Tip: Arrive at/in; get to is the to-pattern.

TRUE — Listen to + object is obligatory in standard English.

Tip: Hear can take a direct object; listen needs to.

FALSE — Wait for the bus; wait cannot take a bare object here.

Tip: Wait for someone/something.

TRUE — Look at correctly directs visual attention.

Tip: Look at / stare at; watch can take a direct object.

FALSE — Talk about the film; talk needs about (or to a person).

Tip: Talk about a topic; discuss a topic (no about).
tasks.solution_overview: Perception and movement verbs often need a preposition English learners drop: arrive at/in, listen to, wait for, look at, talk about.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She goes to work by foot every morning.
They travelled to the coast by train.
The match starts in Monday evening.
I usually read in night when the house is quiet.
We met on a cold Friday afternoon.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — On foot, not by foot.

Tip: By + vehicle (by bus/train/car); on foot is the walking exception.

TRUE — By train correctly names the means of transport.

Tip: By + vehicle is the default transport pattern.

FALSE — On Monday / on Monday evening, not in Monday.

Tip: On + days and dated times; in + months/years/parts of day (in the evening).

FALSE — At night is the fixed time phrase; in night is wrong.

Tip: At night / in the night (rarer); never bare in night.

TRUE — On + day/date phrases is standard.

Tip: On Friday / on Friday afternoon both work.
tasks.solution_overview: Time and transport prepositions are closed sets: by + vehicle, on foot, on + day, at night. Memorise the exceptions rather than translating.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We congratulated her for winning the baking contest.
Don't blame me about the burnt toast.
Thanks for helping me move the sofa.
The hostel provided us with clean towels.
Police charged him of vandalising the bus stop.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Congratulate someone on winning; for is weaker/wrong in exam English after congratulate.

Tip: Congratulate on an achievement.

FALSE — Blame someone for something, not about.

Tip: Blame for / accuse of — different heads, different prepositions.

TRUE — Thank(s) for + gerund/noun is correct.

Tip: Thank for help; thank someone for doing X.

TRUE — Provide someone with something is the classic ditransitive pattern.

Tip: Provide with / supply with; provide something to someone is also possible.

FALSE — Charge someone with an offence, not of.

Tip: Charge with; accuse of — do not mix them.
tasks.solution_overview: Speech-act verbs split carefully: congratulate on, blame for, thank for, provide with, charge with. Mixing for/of/about across these heads is a common trap.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He is keen on early-morning runs along the canal.
She is fond from old jazz records.
They take pride of their community garden.
I'm tired of waiting for the plumber.
He gets bored of the same playlist every day.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Keen on + noun/gerund expresses enthusiasm.

Tip: Keen on ≈ interested in / enthusiastic about.

FALSE — Fond of, not fond from.

Tip: Fond of people and things you like.

FALSE — Take pride in, not pride of.

Tip: Pride in / proud of — related meaning, different prepositions.

TRUE — Tired of + gerund/noun is fixed.

Tip: Tired of doing X; exhausted from effort is a different idea.

FALSE — Prefer bored with (or by) in careful English; bored of is informal/non-standard for many exams.

Tip: Bored with the routine; fed up with is the of-cousin.
tasks.solution_overview: Attitude adjectives and nouns lock to one preposition: keen on, fond of, pride in, tired of, bored with. Near-synonyms do not share prepositions.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: According to the weather app, storms arrive tonight.
We stayed home because of the flooding.
She chose tea instead coffee after dinner.
In addition of stretching, he iced his knee.
As a result of the delay, they missed the opening act.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — According to + source is the reporting preposition phrase.

Tip: According to X; never according with for this meaning.

TRUE — Because of + noun phrase correctly gives a reason.

Tip: Because of + noun; because + clause.

FALSE — Instead of coffee; instead alone cannot take a bare noun like this.

Tip: Instead of X; instead (adverb) stands alone.

FALSE — In addition to stretching, not in addition of.

Tip: In addition to / as well as — both take to, not of.

TRUE — As a result of + noun phrase is a fixed causal pattern.

Tip: As a result of X; as a result (alone) needs a comma and a clause.
tasks.solution_overview: Multi-word prepositions are all-or-nothing: according to, because of, instead of, in addition to, as a result of. Missing or swapped final prepositions make the item false.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She insisted that we leave the campsite before dawn.
The coach discouraged them to swim after dark.
Warm soup helped him recover from the cold.
Nothing will stop her to finish the marathon.
He specialised in marine biology at university.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Insist that + clause is a separate fixed pattern from insist on + -ing.

Tip: Insist that (clause) vs insist on (gerund) — both valid, different frames.

FALSE — Discourage someone from swimming, not to swim.

Tip: Discourage/prevent/keep from + -ing.

TRUE — Recover from an illness is the standard medical collocation.

Tip: Recover from; recover of is wrong.

FALSE — Stop her from finishing / stop her finishing; not stop her to finish for prevention.

Tip: Stop to do = pause in order to; stop from doing = prevent.

TRUE — Specialise in a field is fixed.

Tip: Specialise/major in a subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch verbs that look like they take infinitives but actually take from + -ing (discourage, stop for prevention). Keep insist that and specialise in intact.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I'm used to waking up before sunrise.
She used to waking up before sunrise when she worked nights.
They are accustomed with long bus rides.
He prefers walking to cycling in the city.
We prefer walking than cycling when it rains.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Be used to + gerund means accustomed to a habit.

Tip: Be/get used to + noun/-ing.

FALSE — Used to + base verb for past habits: used to wake, not used to waking.

Tip: Used to V (past habit) ≠ be used to V-ing (accustomed).

FALSE — Accustomed to, not accustomed with.

Tip: Accustomed/used → to.

TRUE — Prefer X to Y correctly compares two options.

Tip: Prefer A to B; not prefer A than B.

FALSE — Prefer … than is wrong; use prefer walking to cycling, or would rather walk than cycle.

Tip: Prefer to; rather than.
highlights: used to waking up before sunrise when
tasks.solution_overview: Separate past-habit used to + V from be used to + -ing, keep accustomed to, and compare preferences with prefer A to B — never prefer … than.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: In spite of the heat, they finished the hike.
In spite the heat, they finished the hike.
Notwithstanding the late start, the choir sounded polished.
She refrained to comment during the argument.
Please refrain from posting spoilers online.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — In spite of + noun phrase equals despite.

Tip: In spite of keeps of; despite drops it.

FALSE — In spite must be followed by of before a noun.

Tip: Never write in spite the… — insert of.

TRUE — Notwithstanding takes a noun phrase with no extra of.

Tip: Notwithstanding X ≈ despite X.

FALSE — Refrain from commenting, not refrain to comment.

Tip: Refrain/abstain from + -ing.

TRUE — Refrain from + gerund is the fixed restraint pattern.

Tip: From + -ing after refrain.
tasks.solution_overview: Contrast markers split: despite / notwithstanding (no of) versus in spite of (needs of). Restraint verbs take from + -ing, not to-infinitives.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The outcome of the experiment depends on temperature.
Access to the roof terrace is restricted after dusk.
She has no intention to cancel the trip.
There is no point of arguing about the score.
What's the point in staying if the museum is closed?
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Depend on correctly links outcome to a condition.

Tip: Outcome of X; depend on Y — two different prepositions in one sentence can both be right.

TRUE — Access to a place is the fixed pattern.

Tip: Access to; entrance to; not access of for places.

FALSE — Intention of cancelling / no intention of -ing is preferred; intention to is often marked wrong in exams.

Tip: Have no intention of doing X.

FALSE — No point in arguing, not point of arguing in this frame.

Tip: No point in + -ing; what's the point of is a related but different pattern.

TRUE — Point in + gerund is acceptable in this rhetorical question.

Tip: Point in / point of both appear; match the whole fixed frame.
tasks.solution_overview: Abstract nouns pick locked prepositions: access to, intention of, point in/of. Do not assume to after every noun that feels "future-facing."

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She was angry with her brother for borrowing her headphones.
He was angry about the cancelled ferry.
They were pleased of the surprise birthday brunch.
I'm delighted with how the garden turned out.
We were surprised from the sudden snowfall.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Angry with a person + for a reason is a solid double pattern.

Tip: Angry with people; angry about situations.

TRUE — Angry about a situation/event is correct.

Tip: About for things; with for people.

FALSE — Pleased with/by, not pleased of.

Tip: Proud of vs pleased with — do not swap.

TRUE — Delighted with a result is natural and grammatical.

Tip: Delighted with/by; delighted to hear that…

FALSE — Surprised by/at, not surprised from.

Tip: Surprised by news; shocked at/by.
tasks.solution_overview: Emotion adjectives split people vs situations (angry with / about) and reject of/from transfers (pleased with, surprised by).

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The soup tastes of garlic and lemon.
This jacket smells like woodsmoke.
She reminded me of my primary-school teacher.
Can you remind me of locking the back door?
Please remind him to bring the picnic blanket.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Taste of a flavour is a fixed sensory pattern.

Tip: Taste of / smell of a substance.

TRUE — Smell like is acceptable for resemblance.

Tip: Smell of a substance; smell like a comparison — both can work.

TRUE — Remind someone of a person/thing (resemblance or memory trigger).

Tip: Remind of a memory; remind to do a duty.

FALSE — For a future action use remind me to lock, not remind me of locking.

Tip: Remind of = memory/resemblance; remind to = instruction.

TRUE — Remind someone to + infinitive correctly issues a prompt.

Tip: Reminder for actions → to + V.
tasks.solution_overview: Sensory of/like patterns are fine; remind splits into of (memory) versus to (future action). Mixing those two frames is the hard trap.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The festival was cancelled owing to high winds.
Owing the high winds, the festival was cancelled.
The hike was postponed due to flooding on the trail.
Due the flooding, the hike was postponed.
Thanks to a clear sky, we saw the meteor shower.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Owing to + noun phrase is a formal causal preposition.

Tip: Owing to = because of.

FALSE — Owing needs to before the noun phrase.

Tip: Never drop to from owing to.

TRUE — Due to + noun is widely accepted as a causal preposition in modern exam English.

Tip: Due to X / because of X.

FALSE — Due the… is incomplete; insert to.

Tip: Due to, not bare due before a noun cause.

TRUE — Thanks to + noun credits a positive cause.

Tip: Thanks to (positive); owing to / due to (neutral/negative).
tasks.solution_overview: Causal multi-word prepositions all keep their final to: owing to, due to, thanks to. Any stripped to is an automatic false.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She accused him for leaving the gate open.
They suspected her of feeding the stray cats.
He was convicted for trespassing on farmland.
The club banned him from using the tennis courts.
Nothing can compensate the loss of the old oak.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Accuse someone of doing, not for.

Tip: Accuse of; blame for.

TRUE — Suspected of + gerund is the fixed collocation.

Tip: Suspected/accused of wrongdoing.

FALSE — Convicted of an offence is the standard legal/exam pattern (for appears in some loose usage but of is safer here).

Tip: Convicted of; charged with.

TRUE — Ban someone from + gerund/noun is correct.

Tip: Ban/prohibit from; forbid someone to is different.

FALSE — Compensate for a loss; compensate cannot take the loss as a bare object in this sense.

Tip: Compensate for damage/loss.
tasks.solution_overview: Fault and restriction vocabulary is preposition-heavy: accuse/suspect/convict of, ban from, compensate for. Swapping for/of or dropping the preposition fails the item.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The plan is contingent on dry weather this weekend.
Approval is contingent of dry weather this weekend.
She prides herself in finishing every crossword.
She takes pride in finishing every crossword.
He is proud for his daughter's science prize.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Contingent on + noun/gerund matches depend on.

Tip: Contingent on conditions.

FALSE — Contingent of is a depend-of style transfer error.

Tip: On, not of, after contingent.

FALSE — Pride oneself on doing, not in, after the reflexive verb.

Tip: Pride oneself on; take pride in — different verbs, different prepositions.

TRUE — Take pride in + gerund is fixed.

Tip: Take pride in / be proud of.

FALSE — Proud of an achievement, not proud for.

Tip: Proud of someone/something.
tasks.solution_overview: Near-identical pride frames diverge: pride oneself on vs take pride in vs be proud of. Contingent follows depend → on, never of.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: By the time we arrived, the café had run out of cups.
The café had run out from cups before noon.
I'm looking forward for the weekend hike.
She objects to being photographed without consent.
He succeeded on repairing the leaky tap.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Run out of + noun is the depletion pattern.

Tip: Run out of supplies; run out (intransitive) for time.

FALSE — Run out from cups is wrong; use run out of.

Tip: Of after run out for materials.

FALSE — Looking forward to the hike, not for.

Tip: Look forward to + noun/-ing.

TRUE — Object to + gerund is correct.

Tip: Object to being/doing; not object against.

FALSE — Succeeded in repairing, not on.

Tip: Succeed in + -ing; insist on is a different verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Close with high-frequency exam traps: run out of, look forward to, object to, succeed in. Wrong satellite prepositions are the only thing that separates TRUE from FALSE here.
